name: Treaty with the Ottawa, etc., 1816 (Treaty of St. Louis)
nations: United Ottawa, Chippewa and Potawatomi of the Illinois and Milwaukee rivers (Bodéwadmi, Odawa, Anishinaabe)
promises: Merchandise delivered at signing and $1,000 in goods a year for twelve years, delivered on the Illinois River no lower than Peoria (Article 2).

The United States relinquished to the tribes the part of the 1804 Sac and Fox cession north of a line west from the south end of Lake Michigan, except three leagues square at the mouth of the Wisconsin River and other tracts the President might reserve, not exceeding five leagues square in all (Article 2).
The tribes could hunt and fish on the ceded land while it remained the property of the United States (Article 1).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found the Potawatomi held recognized title to Royce Area 78 (783,150.47 acres in northeastern Illinois, including the Chicago portage), set its value at $1.15 an acre, or $900,623.04, credited the $12,000 disbursed under the treaty, and entered a final award of $888,623.04 to the Potawatomi Tribe as constituted in 1816.

landTaken: Royce Area 78, 783,150.47 acres (stipulated by the parties, Commission order of 1978). The Potawatomi did not claim further compensation for Royce Area 77.
compensation: $12,000 credited as consideration; final award of $888,623.04 in 1978.
today: The value was fixed by a 1975 stipulation tying Area 78 to the per-acre value the Commission later found for Royce Area 98 in Dockets 15-D et al.; the stipulation concerned how value would be measured, not a compromise of the claim. The Commission's 1973 title decision is 32 Ind. Cl. Comm. 400.

nationVoice.summary: The Band's history says the Potawatomi lived in what is now Wisconsin, southern Michigan, northern Indiana and northern Illinois, that as the frontier moved west boundary arguments and land cessions became a way of life, and that the 1833 Treaty of Chicago then set the terms for removing the Potawatomi from the Great Lakes.

openQuestions: The final award order does not use the word unconscionable; the auditor may want to confirm the legal basis of the award in the 1973 opinion before this is cited publicly.
Ottawa and Chippewa claims in Dockets 13-K, 18-P and 40-I were dismissed in 1973 (Commission index); the order was not opened.
No nation statement about this treaty was found.

Audit 2026-11-08: the second promise now includes the three leagues square at the mouth of the Wisconsin River that Article 2 also excepted. The award stands as found: the 1978 orders award fair market value less the $12,000 consideration on a recognized-title cession; neither order nor the 1973 title opinion uses the word unconscionable.

plain.promised: The United States promised $1,000 in goods a year for twelve years, gave back to the tribes part of an earlier cession, and said they could hunt and fish on the ceded land while it stayed US property.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1978 that the Potawatomi held recognized title to 783,150.47 acres in northeastern Illinois, including the Chicago portage, worth $900,623.04, against $12,000 paid under the treaty.
plain.today: The Commission entered a final award of $888,623.04 to the Potawatomi in 1978. Whether it was paid has not been traced.
